overview: The atlas calls this layer “Nitassinan (Innu),” but Nitassinan is an Innu relationship with homeland, not a state founded in 1492. Institut Tshakapesh translates the name as “our land,” describes seasonal movement across Labrador and northeastern Quebec, and says a fixed frontier did not belong to that mobile culture. The atlas nevertheless draws a polygon for 1492 to 1500. It includes Sheshatshiu, Natuashish, Labrador City, Schefferville, Kawawachikamach, Pessamit, and Mashteuiatsh, while excluding several eastern communities; it also overlaps other atlas layers. Those pixels cannot show all residence, kinship, travel, use, or authority. Evidence near 1492 is uneven. Archaeological sites illuminate long use of particular places, but cultural labels and ancestry remain debated. Later community teaching, oral history, ethnography, museum objects, and current institutions reveal knowledge and continuity only when their dates are kept visible. They help discuss food, housing, family, children, medicine, and sanitation without being silently projected backward. The 1500 repaint is likewise no cultural ending: it is one map seam within a longer Indigenous history.

periods.title: The atlas opens a map layer
periods.summary: The exact id first appears in the 1492 snapshot with approximate dates. No source identifies 1492 as a founding, migration, treaty, or conquest year. This first one-year band is an evidence-reading division imposed by the card format, not a claim that Innu history changed at its edges.

periods.title: Ancient camps resist a point origin
periods.summary: Kameshtashtan contains camps dated at least 6,500 years old and later work reports an earliest date of 7,300 years. Parks Canada links the landscape to Mushuau Innu history while describing layered evidence. These deep dates reject a 1492 origin without assigning every earlier occupant a simple modern label.

periods.title: Point Revenge ancestry is disputed
periods.summary: A 2026 peer-reviewed reassessment tests three hypotheses about the Point Revenge complex. Its results favor a return to Newfoundland in the early sixteenth century and a relationship with Beothuk traditions. This period therefore marks an unresolved attribution problem, not a securely named Innu archaeological phase in 1494.

periods.title: Southern sites show long passage
periods.summary: Excavations in the Sainte-Marguerite basin found occupations extending across roughly four millennia, including homes, portage passage, and stone from many sources. The evidence supports long Indigenous use and connections on the Cote-Nord. It cannot assign a sharply bounded Nitassinan government to this single atlas year.

periods.title: Routes matter more than year lines
periods.summary: The Meshikamau-shipu route joins Sheshatshiu to the interior across about 330 kilometres of rivers, lakes, camps, portages, birthplaces, and burial places. Some camps date back 3,500 years. This evidence describes enduring movement through particular places, while the 1496 boundary is only a narrative partition.

periods.title: Cabot does not prove an Innu meeting
periods.summary: Nametau records Cabot’s 1497 voyage as a trigger for later fisheries, but documents Breton use of fishing grounds in 1506 and Cartier’s encounter with Breton crews in 1534. The page calls early Innu contact highly likely; it does not document an Innu person meeting Cabot in 1497.

periods.title: Sparse finds are not empty land
periods.summary: A 1997 Innu Nation archaeological project found that small, dispersed precontact camps can be hard to detect and that early-contact sites remained elusive. The author warns against treating scarcity as proof of transient occupation. This band records that evidentiary limit, not a population event in 1498.

periods.title: The endpoint is a repaint
periods.summary: At the 1500 snapshot the exact id disappears. Some tested places receive the broader innu label, others subarctic-forest-hunter-gatherers, and Mashteuiatsh algonquin. These are atlas category changes, not evidence that Nitassinan, Innu families, or land relationships ended on January 1, 1500.

sections.title: Read the atlas label as a bounded visualization

items.text: The repository indexes nitassinan-innu only from 1492 to 1500, marks both dates approximate, and stores one matching feature in one border file. No card or researched override existed before this packet. These facts define the visualization target; they do not establish an Indigenous state or historical lifespan.

The decoded feature is one polygon with one ring and 130 stored positions. Its bounding box runs approximately from 74.14 degrees west to 55.66 degrees west and 47.74 to 56.88 degrees north. Those geometry facts describe a generalized map object, not a surveyed Innu frontier.

Representative tests place Sheshatshiu, Natuashish, Labrador City, Schefferville, Kawawachikamach, Pessamit, and Mashteuiatsh inside, but Uashat, Mani-Utenam, Ekuanitshit, Nutashkuan, Unamen Shipu, and Pakua Shipi outside. The mismatch with living community geography is direct evidence against treating the shape as timeless Nitassinan.

At Schefferville and Kawawachikamach the target overlaps atlas layers called Inuit, St'aschinuw Naskapi, and Nunavik. Quebec’s current profile identifies a distinct Naskapi Nation, language, and village at Kawawachikamach. Layer overlap cannot erase that identity or convert neighboring peoples into one polity.

The imported summary came from Wikipedia and describes Nitassinan as a territory. This packet replaces that lead with located community and institutional evidence. It also keeps related ids separate: innu, Montagnais Innu, Naskapi Innu, Inuit, Nunatsiavut, NunatuKavut, and St'aschinuw are not aliases for this polygon.

sections.title: Use archaeology without assigning easy ancestry

items.text: Parks Canada describes Kameshtashtan as a Mushuau Innu cultural landscape with ancient camps, births, deaths, routes, and oral histories. The heritage record reports camps at least 6,500 years old and ongoing work reaching 7,300. It supports deep place use, while “ancestors” remains a carefully contextualized attribution.

The Sainte-Marguerite project recorded 67 sites; selected excavations identified repeated occupations, homes, and passage along a difficult river route over about 4,000 years. Nametau presents these as evidence of ancient Innu presence, but quoted archaeological interpretation still speaks broadly of Amerindian groups and different cultural spheres.

A 1996 heritage report used the then-common model linking the Point Revenge complex with Innu history near Natuashish. Its dates and artifact descriptions remain useful as an older scholarly position. The attribution itself cannot be repeated as settled fact because newer research directly reopens the relationship.

The 2026 Point Revenge study says some archaeologists had treated the relationship with known Indigenous populations as settled. It tests competing hypotheses with site locations and diagnostic tools, then favors links to Newfoundland and Beothuk history. That conclusion makes a simple “Point Revenge equals Innu” statement unsafe.

Archaeological names classify assemblages, not self-identifying nations. The Point Revenge reassessment concerns material patterns and population hypotheses; it does not negate Innu oral history, current identity, or other evidence of long homeland relationships. The responsible card preserves both the scientific dispute and the limits of what artifacts alone can name.

sections.title: Follow routes, exchanges, and place knowledge

items.text: Meshikamau-shipu follows rivers and lakes for about 330 kilometres between Sheshatshiu and the interior. Parks Canada records camps, portages, birth and burial places, walking, paddling, and boating. Distant stone at sites indicates long-distance travel and exchange, although no single route defines all of Nitassinan.

A Sainte-Marguerite site sat beside a long portage around rapids and contained 21 stone types, suggesting relationships west, northwest, and north. Movement joined coast, interior lakes, and neighboring networks. Archaeology demonstrates connection and repeated passage more securely than it reveals political borders or the names travelers used.

Interior Labrador surveys found precontact sites scarce but repeatedly present, while stone sources including Ramah chert imply long-distance trade and travel. Schwarz stresses strong coastal survey bias and poor interior visibility. Distribution maps therefore reflect where archaeologists looked as well as where people moved, camped, and exchanged materials.

Since 1976, Innu elders, hunters, and experts from Sheshatshiu and Davis Inlet have mapped routes and named places across giant floor maps. Natural Resources Canada says nearly 1,200 names were compiled with histories of camps, gatherings, births, burials, hunting, and fishing. This is dated collaborative research, not a 1492 gazetteer.

Innu Nation shared more than 400 pronunciation recordings with Canada’s geographical names database, and nearly 500 mapped names became official in Newfoundland and Labrador. This is a modern achievement in language and cartography. It also shows why a living toponymic network conveys more than one atlas polygon can.

sections.title: Read food evidence by place and date

items.text: At Kameshtashtan, camps occur near caribou drive locations and water crossings. Food-storage caches and crushed caribou bone in hearths provide material evidence of processing and respectful practice. The site record ties food to one cultural landscape; it is not a menu for every Innu family in 1492.

The same landscape sits between boreal forest and subarctic tundra. Parks Canada lists migrating caribou, waterfowl, fish, ptarmigan, and small mammals around the lake. This ecological range helps explain seasonal choices, but modern abundance descriptions and long archaeological spans cannot supply harvest totals for the card’s eight-year window.

Nametau’s elder-to-youth teaching page describes valued caribou portions for guests, extracting fat from broken bones, wrapping food in birch bark, and placing remains on a cache respectfully. The page preserves living teaching in a 2010 museum project; it is comparative evidence, not a verbatim fifteenth-century account.

The caribou page organizes knowledge across fall, winter, spring, and summer activities, including geese, salmon, ducks, seafood, seals, and planning. Its seasonal sequence is useful because it resists reducing Innu subsistence to one animal. The page does not establish that every regional group followed an identical annual round.

Armitage’s late twentieth-century account says women and children fished, gathered berries, and took small game within seasonal camps. It records household labor in a much later period and under changed conditions. The comparison can broaden daily life, but it cannot assign the same roles unchanged to 1492.

Nametau lists stone points, lances, harpoons, axes, adzes, scrapers, and strikers from archaeological sites. It also warns that wood, antler, leather, and most bone objects seldom survive. A stone-heavy collection therefore cannot be treated as a complete inventory of technology, clothing, containers, or play.

Later illustrations and photographs show shelters framed with poles and covered with birch bark, conifer boughs, or hides. Nametau also describes rawhide-and-birch snowshoes, birchbark canoes joined with root cord, wooden sleds, shovels, oars, and traps. These nineteenth-century comparisons require dating, not silent back-projection.

A Smithsonian object record identifies Labrador snowshoes as Montagnais Innu, collected by Frank Speck in 1924. Catalog 13/3080 specifies wood, hide thong, carving, and two plaiting techniques. The exact object documents skilled construction in 1924; it does not prove that its design was unchanged in 1492.

Smithsonian catalog 13/3201 is a Labrador Montagnais Innu cup-and-pin game collected in 1924. Bone, hide thong, and deer tail were incised and perforated. It is a welcome glimpse of play as well as craft, kept within its collection date instead of being promoted to fifteenth-century evidence.

Armitage describes twentieth-century hunting camps chosen for water, fuel, fish, and boughs, commonly containing two to eight tents with poles, canvas, and stoves. That account explains practical camp decisions in living memory. Canvas and metal stoves make its late date obvious and guard against reconstructing a 1492 dwelling.

sections.title: Keep families and regional groups visible

items.text: A guide written by Innu health staff says children have been raised within large extended-family groups in which grandparents, older siblings, aunts, uncles, and other kin may carry roles as important as birth parents. This is community testimony about continuity; it is not a household census from 1492.

The same guide recalls that before permanent village settlement in the 1960s, extended families shared responsibility for raising children into competent adults. The statement connects parenting with relationships and collective work. Because it is retrospective and centered on Labrador communities, the card does not assume identical arrangements everywhere centuries earlier.

Parks Canada says Meshikamau travel brought families from across Nitassinan to gathering places and maintained social ties while people harvested resources. Families from Sheshatshiu still use interior camps. The record supports a network of movement and reunion, not an isolated household model or a single centralized capital.

Armitage’s later account describes camps containing several households and summer gatherings in which dispersed families reunited. It also records differentiated work in camp without reducing social life to hunting alone. These twentieth-century observations offer comparison, while warfare, trade, missions, and settlement had already altered circumstances profoundly.

The 1996 relocation study begins with families settling at Utshimassit in 1967 under provincial and church initiative, then seeking a mainland move after serious site problems. This modern history explains why current community locations and services cannot be read backward as the settlement pattern or political geography of 1492.

sections.title: Teach children through practice and institutions

items.text: Innu health staff describe children learning through daily observation, play, and participation: a toddler might watch an older sister pluck a goose, then gradually take responsibility. The guide also says work was not rigidly divided by gender; boys might sew, while girls snared, hunted, or cut wood.

The guide also records colonial disruption: priests challenged spiritual practice, governments promoted permanent settlement, and daily school attendance displaced elders and parents as teachers. This is a community account of twentieth-century change. It should inform the card’s ending without turning 1492 into an untouched or frozen cultural baseline.

Mamu Tshishkutamashutau Innu Education says it has held jurisdiction over Labrador Innu schooling since 2009. Two schools in Sheshatshiu and Natuashish honor language, traditions, and culture under trustees selected by the communities. This current institution demonstrates living educational self-determination, not a survival unchanged from 1492.

MTIE’s curriculum catalogue includes Innu-aimun activities, beginner lessons, teaching vocabulary, early-literacy resources, spelling guidance, typing support, and Innu social studies. The variety shows language work joining oral, land-based, and written learning today. A current resource list cannot be used as evidence for fifteenth-century classrooms.

The place-name project began with elders, hunters, and experts walking over large floor maps and identifying places and routes. Its records attach stories to camps, gatherings, births, burials, hunting, and fishing. This collaborative practice is both knowledge transmission and cartography, while its documented research date begins in 1976.

sections.title: Discuss medicine and care without inventing 1492 practice

items.text: In 2006 and 2007, an Innu Traditional Knowledge Committee discussed nutshimiu-natukun, translated as “country medicine,” derived from plants and animals. The report says systematic documentation lay outside its scope and its examples were incomplete. It offers dated living knowledge, not a remedy list verified for 1492.

One committee participant declined to describe medicines in detail because knowledge had previously been taken and commercialized by a non-Innu person. That refusal is evidence about consent and knowledge governance. A responsible public card therefore names the medicine tradition and its limits without reproducing formulas or treating protected expertise as open data.

Participants described medicines as differing in strength and associated some strong medicines with river valleys. The report presents these ideas as committee knowledge and translation, not clinical efficacy trials. Nothing in the selected record securely dates a named treatment to 1492, so the card preserves the gap rather than fabricating continuity.

A 2009 federal evaluation says Innu interviewees understood community healing as long-term, holistic, collaborative, and needing an Innu definition. It assesses modern programs responding to colonial harms and crisis. That institutional evidence belongs to recent history and cannot stand in for precontact diagnoses, practitioners, or access to care.

The same evaluation records maternal and child health, mental-health, addictions, safe-house, wellness, and culturally appropriate programs in Sheshatshiu and Natuashish. These are important current forms of care. Their presence demonstrates adaptation and community action; it says nothing direct about patient outcomes or medical organization in the fifteenth century.

sections.title: Mark the water, sanitation, and toilet evidence gap

items.text: Schwarz inventories late twentieth-century camps with tent frames, hearths, firewood scaffolds, a medicine bottle, washbasin, storage platforms, and in-ground fish freezers. The survey does not identify a securely precontact toilet or latrine. That narrow documentary absence must not be inflated into proof that people lacked sanitation practices.

The same survey explains why absence is difficult to interpret: small camps, shallow deposits, organic remains, vegetation, erosion, flooding, and coastal research bias reduce visibility. Archaeology can miss perishable waste-management arrangements. A careful card reports “not documented in these sources,” rather than declaring that fifteenth-century Innu used no toilets.

At Utshimassit after 1967, drinking water was scarce and the site could not support a sewer system, contributing to health and social problems. Bibeau records this as a consequence of a modern government-directed settlement on an island. It is not evidence for water or waste arrangements in mobile camps five centuries earlier.

The 2002 move to Natuashish enabled clean water and indoor plumbing, according to the federal healing-strategy evaluation. This sharp infrastructure change belongs to recent colonial and community history. It also warns against asking a modern municipal question of a 1492 mobile landscape without direct archaeological or oral evidence.

Material-culture evidence has a preservation bias: Nametau notes that wood, antler, leather, and other organic objects usually disappear while stone survives. The selected sources preserve no secure 1492 toilet form, waste pit, bathing installation, or drinking-water treatment. The honest result is a bounded evidence gap, not an invented fixture.

Secure modern written-language sample: “Nitassinan.” The current Innu language lesson prints it in Roman orthography and translates it “Our territory.” The language is Innu-aimun; the displayed transliteration is likewise Nitassinan because no different historical script is being transliterated. This sample documents living writing, not a text from 1492.

No selected source provides a securely dated 1492 Innu inscription, manuscript, or recorded utterance. The lesson’s Roman letters are the actual modern web rendering, not reconstructed fifteenth-century glyphs. Its translation scope is only the phrase “Our territory”; it should not be expanded into a sentence or treated as a facsimile.

Nametau connects Cabot’s 1497 voyage to expanding Atlantic fisheries, but its first firm local comparison is Breton use of fishing grounds in 1506. The page says French fishermen were highly likely to be the first Europeans to contact Innu. Possibility is not a named encounter, date, person, or trading event.

Cartier encountered Breton fishing crews west of modern Blanc-Sablon in 1534, and larger French and Basque activity followed. These post-card anchors make later contact increasingly plausible. They do not justify moving documented commerce into 1497 or portraying contact as one simultaneous event across the entire atlas polygon.

A modern agreement-in-principle would transfer Innu-origin artifacts to an Innu government, protect burial and spiritual sites, require consultation before archaeology, and assign conservation responsibilities. This is present-day legal work toward heritage authority. It is an achievement of living governance, not proof that the 1492 polygon was a comparable state.

ending.text: The card ends at 1500 because the exact atlas id disappears there, not because Nitassinan or Innu people ended. The next snapshot repaints tested places with several labels: innu at Sheshatshiu, Natuashish, and Happy Valley-Goose Bay; subarctic-forest-hunter-gatherers farther west and south; and algonquin at Mashteuiatsh. By 1530 the atlas introduces Montagnais Innu and Naskapi Innu labels. None is a documented legal succession from this polygon, so the successor list stays empty. Later colonial settlement, schooling, resource development, and infrastructure deeply changed life, while current Innu institutions demonstrate active language, education, and community authority. Mamu Tshishkutamashutau Innu Education, established in 2009, operates community-governed schools in Sheshatshiu and Natuashish that honor Innu language, land, and culture. The appropriate status is continuity: a map category stops, while a living people and homeland relationship continue beyond its seam.
